en: I have no power for worship, nor devotion at your feet, nor detachment from sense objects, nor capacity for the yoga of meditation;
thus always reflecting in my mind, I perform the worship of the Primal Power with the flowers of her beautiful words. 1.

Oh, let your mind constantly become fulfilled by contemplating the ocean of reddish nectar, its interior crowded with ships filled with heaps of gold and carrying multitudes of deities, adorned with jewel-bearing mountains, and filling the sky with masses of surging, restless waves. || 2 ||

We pay homage to that island, which clearly makes the sky appear as if covered on all sides by masses of rainbows through the flashes of luster shimmering from its network of brilliant jewels; where all the deer remain motionless, intent on listening to the songs resounding from the faces of the throngs of celestial nymphs seated upon its lofty peaks.

Contemplate for a long time the Nandana grove, which is filled with the fragrance of jasmine, campaka, pāṭala, and other flowers; where mango trees resound with the "kuhū" calls of cuckoos whose throats are thrilled by the sound of the syllable *hrīṃ*;
where fragrant sandalwood forests have appeared; which is pleasing to the sight; and which is made restless by the fluttering of darting bees. 4.

With its ground reddened by falling pollen, its trees high with blossoming flowers, drinking in the rays of the moon and sun, and enchanting the ears with the warbling of bees, parrots, and flocks of cuckoos—may this king of gardens truly manifest within my heart. 5.

Obeisance to you, whose radiance destroys the darkness moving through the beautiful gates and cities; whose splendor is like a great necklace of light bearing the weight of shimmering archways; who bestows the further shore of saṃsāra while shining with a golden necklace upon the circle of the earth; O golden rampart, the playground for the minds of your devoted followers! || 6 ||

May this glorious Maṇimaṇḍapa shine incessantly in my mind—it which possesses the splendor of a shimmering canopy fashioned by a mass of rising radiance; it which perfumes the intermediate quarters of the sky with the incense of excellent black agallochum; and it which is perpetually attended by hosts of deities who have come for service.
In one place made like twilight by a mass of rays from towering rubies, in another made like the night by the brilliance of shimmering emeralds,
and in yet another made like moonlight by the luster of large pearls suspended in the center— O Mother, we ever revere your beautiful and glorious jeweled temple.

Beholding the circles of light radiating from the emeralds shimmering in the lofty dwellings, the horses—mistaking them for patches of ground covered with fresh grass and thus spurred on by burgeoning excitement—have led the chariot of the Sun onto a wrong path; alas, the charioteer, his hand trembling as he struggles with the reins, reaches the mountain peak only with great difficulty.
In the sky, enamored by the streams of luster rising from the jeweled mansions, the chariots of the sun— suspecting it to be the final twilight—
finally emerge with great difficulty from the jewel-palaces, accompanied by the sounds of the charioteers' "huṃ" cries as they slacken their pace and grow indignant.
Were these many jewels offered with devotion by the ocean, or were they fashioned by Viśvakarman from the Rohaṇa mountain for his dwelling?
O Girijā, it is understood: when Śambhu was surely gratified by you with a mere fraction of a sidelong glance, he danced, and rows of gems were strewn about by the hoods of the serpent-king.

O Mother, this jeweled pavilion shines as you prepare to depart, being joyfully awaited by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the other gods, who have dismounted from their vehicles at a distance, whose crowns are bowed low, who join their palms in reverence, and whose senses are restrained with great effort.

May your jeweled pavilion, with its resounding mṛdaṅgas and kāhala drums, with throngs of singing kinnarīs, dancing celestial maidens, and commenced auspicious rites; with its multitude of excellent attendants and circles of joyful devotees, be for my constant delight. (13)

May this jeweled pavilion always bring me auspiciousness here— a place filled with women adorned in variegated garments and ornaments, their minds intent on their own duties amidst the bustle of entering and exiting, while they offer devotion to the rows of deities stationed outside.

Adorned with gold and jewels, wearing variegated garments, holding golden staffs, and having obstructed all other deities, let my mind go to your lofty archway, presided over by countless beautiful women standing before it. (15)

Having meditated within the lotus of my heart upon Indra and the other lords of the directions, together with their retinues, bearing their weapons, and assuming female forms stationed in their respective quarters;

and remembering the lotus joined with the Earth goddess by the stream of the venerable Vasudhārā from the conch—I bow with love to Kāma, the beloved of Rati, and I worship his companion, Vasantaka. 16.

Worshipping Sarasvatī and the others who stand near the door, singing most sweetly with their lutes and uttering the sound "huṃ," I bow at the entrance to the Lord of the hosts of gods, who is intoxicated with passion; I worship Mātaṅgī, who is maddened by passion, clad in black garments, and adorned with shimmering pearls. 17.

In my mind, I remember the daughter of the Mātaṅgas, her limbs dark and tender as musk, her body languid from the intoxication of drinking Kādambarī wine, and a jeweled lute pressed against her left breast. 18.
With my mass of hair disheveled, the display of my garments cast aside, eyes clouded with intoxication, and shining with spotless ornaments—
while contemplating your lotus-feet, O Veil-like Goddess (Tiraskariṇī), I render this assembly of animals utterly bewildered and filled with longing.

I praise your female messengers, whose eyes roll from the intoxicating juices of wine, who are the slayers of fierce demons, and whose minds have entered into your devotees; their forms shine with a mass of luster like freshly applied collyrium, and they bear skulls and tridents.

O Girijā, I bow to that jeweled palace, which is resplendent with four doors; its interior is graced by new jars whose mouths are adorned with shallow bowls shining like lamps, their expansive forms manifesting the sprouts of eternal speech; and it possesses the beauty of door-panels shimmering with clusters of various gems set in gold.

May the interior of the glorious pavilion—the interior which possesses a seat of spread red woolen cloth, is provided with offerings of flowers, is made beautiful by many shining jewel-lamps, is adorned with a magnificent royal canopy, and resounds with the humming of swarms of bees gathering in excitement at the sweet fragrance of rising incense—constantly bestow auspiciousness upon me. (22)

I worship the Supreme Deity who has manifested within the lotus of my heart— she who is seated upon a throne fashioned of gold by five pretas, resplendent with clusters of jewels, spread with a most excellent covering of red and white cloth, fragrant with flowers, and providing the comfort of a divine pillow.

Beholding the Supreme Goddess at dawn—she whose form is beautiful and charming with every limb, who has just arisen, her lotus-face lovely with a yawn, her three eyes rolling from the intoxication of honey-wine, and honoring with her glance all the friends gathered nearby for service—I consider my birth to have achieved its highest purpose. (24)

O Girijā, when the resounding blast of the multitude of musical instruments stationed upon the lofty archway has burst forth, and when the devotees have performed full prostrations with their heads touching the ground,
I shall offer you a brilliant *nīrājana* ceremony at dawn, illuminated by vessels filled with a collection of various gems.
I offer water for your feet at your feet, and likewise water for honor (arghya) for your hands; O Mother, partake of the sweet honey-mixture (madhuparka) with its pure streams.

Perform the ritual rinsing of the mouth (ācamana) with the pure water of the Gaṅgā prepared by me; O Beloved of the Lord, fulfill my purpose with your glance by accepting this prostration with eight limbs (sāṣṭāṅga-praṇipāta).
"O Mother, look at your lotus-face in the spotlessly clear mirror I have offered; O Goddess, accept this tooth-stick accompanied by water from the Gaṅgā.
Wiping your face, which has been thoroughly cleansed, with a soft cloth, quickly accept it, O Mother, and savor that sweet betel-roll. (27)

Place your lotus-foot upon the jeweled sandals and proceed slowly to the bathing chamber, supported by the lotus-hands of your friends. O Great Goddess, O Treasure of Compassion, cast even a slight glance at these deities stationed on both sides, who are longing for the fall of your sidelong look.
Behold my bathhouse, encircled by a screen of gold and jewels, adorned with a wide, crimson canopy, and attended by all the waiting maids ready for service. (29)

Come to the bathing hall of the Great Consort of Supreme Śiva— a place vast with equipment such as crystal bathing pedestals and lattices of golden jars, where rows of bees are intoxicated by the fragrance, the crimson canopy glitters, and the Gandharvas sing sweetly.

I bow to your maidservants, O Mother, who possess full and lofty breasts, faces like the shining full moon, and are adorned with jewels and gold; who are draped in shimmering fine garments; and who hold in their hands golden bathing jars, soft cloths for rubbing, fragrant powders, scented oils, and combs. (31)

May the Blessed One, the Supreme Goddess, shine in my heart—she who, having slowly approached a crystal pedestal, removed her ornaments; who cast off her bodice and donned a crimson upper garment; and who, setting aside her braid with a comb, was slightly arranging her hair.
O Girijā, accept this massage prepared with gentle oil; have yourself anointed with unguents made from saffron, aloe-wood resin, and sandalwood.
O Goddess, look here before you at the circle of celestial maidens dancing, while they are joyfully surrounded by the songs of lovely Kinnara women and the sounding of musical instruments.
Having girded their loins, those bath-attendants— endowed with high and full breasts, carrying golden jars bound with clusters of jewels,
and trailed by swarms of bees greedy for the fragrance of the fragrant water issuing forth— waited upon her from all sides with humility.

O Girijā, with fragrant aloe-wood juices, with scented musk-water, with the highly perfumed waters of yakṣakardama, as well as with saffron-water, with flower-water, with the waters of all sacred fords, and with abundant camphor-water, I perform this bath for you; please accept it with devotion. 35.
I am wiping each limb with a pure cloth; I perform a thorough rubbing of the long mass of hair, which has been perfumed with the finest incenses.
Having set up a curtain drawn by a group of female friends, O Great Lady devoted to the protection of your devotees, who possess the luster of jewels, let the bathing garment be removed.

O Caṇḍikā, I offer you a thick, yellow *caṇḍātaka* garment; O beautiful one, dear as life to the Lord of the Mountain, accept this fine and smooth cloth, radiant with the luster of abundant vermilion, and I present you with a blue bodice, brilliant with the lovely splendor of goldwork inlaid with pearls and various gems.

O Consort of the Lord of the Mountain, proceed now to the pavilion of ornaments, having quickly and gracefully taken hold of your friend’s shoulder with your hand— your hair disheveled as it covers the region of your shoulder, and your feet resting upon sandals resplendent with clusters of jewels.

O Kātyāyanī, occupy the golden lion-throne placed within the pavilion of great ornaments, which is surrounded by your circle of female companions and filled with the radiance of shimmering pearl necklaces set upon floors of polished gold that flash like a multitude of rainbows.
Having gently smoothed the mass of hair with the tip of a fine comb and fashioned a beautiful, pure parting adorned with a line of vermilion,
I shall clearly braid this tress— its curls knotted with pearls and its ends bound with jeweled golden threads and a sprig topped with a cluster of pearls.
O Great Goddess, I offer this crest-jewel, which, with its mass of hair illuminated by its own luster, creates the illusion of a shimmering gem upon the head of the serpent of your hanging braid. 41.
O Mṛḍānī, we salute that head of yours which bears the crest-jewel, wherein the orb of the sun is as if suddenly imprisoned by the darkness of your braided hair as it takes refuge within. 42.

O Bhavānī, I offer this radiant forehead ornament, which is densely filled with the luster of shimmering gems set in gold upon its own center, resplendent on all sides with clusters of hanging pearls, and intensely meditated upon by Bhava with eyes fixed in steady concentration.

O Goddess, let this divine collyrium, surpassing a golden probe, be applied to your long, restless lotus-eyes— which, intoxicated by the drink of honey-wine, eclipse the beauty of fish, lotuses, and wagtails, and indeed mimic the luster of the arrows of Kāma that pierce the mind of the Enemy of Love.

O Girijā, please accept this nose-ornament given by me—a beauty made lovely by the luster of a central ruby, illuminated by pearls and gems, surpassing the splendor of Lakṣmī when she stands between Venus, Jupiter, and the Sun; and which, with the spreading radiance of its elevated bimba-like lip, makes the pearls appear as if they were the earth.

Place upon your shoulder a pair of golden earrings, radiant at their edges with rising rubies, which appear like two solar discs joined together as if in rivalry with the halo formed by the stars around the cool-rayed moon. 46.
O Girijā, I offer this neck-ornament, its center encased in three beads fashioned from excellent emerald, ruby, and diamond, and adorned with an expansive, pure pearl.

O Mother, O Supreme Śivā, place upon the expanse of your chest this four-sided throne, its neck resplendent with ornaments from various lands whose radiant circles of light emanate from clusters of gems, adorned with strings of pure pearls, beautiful with the luster of a central ruby and surrounded by a multitude of pearls at its edges.

May that triad of necklaces, fashioned from pearls, rubies, and radiant emeralds, shine eternally within your heart—you who are a devotee of the Supreme Śiva—like the glorious Triveṇī confluence, which, with its ever-moving nets of waves of splendor, causes the purity of the inner mind to submerge as it flows over one another. 49.

O Goddess Durgā, place upon your pair of arms this pair of golden bracelets, which are like lotus-stalks for your hand-lotuses, which possess a shimmering web of luster, which shine with stainless beauty, which captivate the eyes of the Lord as they gleam, and which are illuminated by the rays of various gems. 50.

O Mother, Consort of Maheśa, I place this pair of armlets upon the base of your arms, which is beautified by clusters of hanging white silk ribbons and resplendent with necklaces set with shimmering gems.

O Great Goddess, behold at the base of your hand this row of bracelets, fashioned from sapphires with their own spread rays, surpassing swarms of intoxicated bees clinging to lotus stalks, and endowed with two bangles inlaid with clusters of gems.
I offer a shimmering golden *taitṛpālikā*— beautiful with its many strings of jewels tied together and adorned with clusters of soft blue silk— to the one who precedes the bracelet.
Like a basin fashioned by the flower-bowed god for young coral creepers, let this ring, offered by me, be slowly placed upon your fingers. 54.

I offer this girdle, set with various gems, which captivates the heart of the Lord with its incessant, sweet tinkling; it resembles a cluster of jingling small bells shaken against the temples of the rutting elephants of the God of Love that were conquered by Him. 55.
I present this waist-band, fashioned of gold, adorned with clusters of excellent hanging pearls, radiant with its two gleaming golden loops, and set with many strings of precious gems. (56)

May the swan find delight in your lotus-feet, which dispel the dense morning heat with the mud of crushed red lac, whose charming anklets sound like rows of emerald gems, and which are variegated by streams of luster rising from rubies.

O Ambika, place upon Your lotus feet this golden girdle, which is beautified by an excellent cluster of white silk ribbons tied fast, which is charming with its sweet tinkling sound, which utterly deludes the mind of Śiva, and which is variegated by the stainless luster of a multitude of brilliant gems.
I offer to your lotus-feet this pair of ruby anklets, which are colored by the shimmering natural glow [of your feet] and whose tinkling is perceived by your circle of friends. 59.

O Great Goddess, I bow to the circle of your toenails resting upon your lotus feet— reddened by the abundance of fresh liquid lac, appearing like a succession of lunar orbs made crimson at the end of the day as they have come to worship your lotus feet.

O you who take delight in the Supreme Śiva, I offer upon the throne of your neck a garland of shimmering white water-lilies, variegated with large blossoms glowing in red, white, and yellow, diligently perfumed by celestial women with agallochum smoke and divine incenses, and made resonant with the humming songs of swarms of bees blinded by its rising fragrance.
Accept this supreme nectar placed within a golden vessel; offer a pure betel-roll to Your lotus-like face, O Mother!
Behold Your own lotus-face in the stainless mirror; place Your lotus-feet, O beautiful one, upon the jeweled sandals.
Gently rising from her lion-throne while holding her handmaid by the hand, her ornaments and garments shimmering as she moved with a charming gait like that of a softly cooing swan—
may that Daughter of the Mountain, who was praised by the Creator with Upaniṣadic verses that convey supreme bliss as she proceeded toward the assembly hall, attain stability within my heart.

As Ambā moved, the entire retinue moved along with her; as the weight of her golden creeper-like ornaments was carried away with speed, the jeweled chamber resounded with a sharp *jhaṇajhaṇita* from the loud *jhaṇat*-sounds produced by the rhythmic impact of her high-stepping feet.

I bow to that Light, whose singular nature is pure consciousness and bliss, who gladdened Śambhu as he emerged from the inner chamber; a chamber where the hosts of immortals were cleared away by female attendants moving before him with waving vetra-staves, their limbs adorned with shimmering ornaments and garments, while the celestial beauties blocked the way on all sides.

"Brahmā falls at the soles of her feet; here is Viṣṇu bowing before her; Śambhu is casting a sidelong glance; look at the Lord of the Gods standing afar!"—when the maidservants speak thus, may the Blessed Lady, bestowing honor with both her eyes as is fitting, be for my prosperity.

May the beloved of Maheśa protect the world; she who, as she gazes upon the hosts of gods who have suddenly come within her sight, slowly offers her lotus-foot upon the path, while being announced from every direction by beautiful female bards moving slowly around her, each calling out her name with longing.
Some are in front, a few on either side, others behind, some have set out into the sky, and still others are stationed in the various directions;

having gradually cleared a path through the crowd, those gods, repeatedly performing prostrations with their staff-like limbs before you, O Daughter of the Mountain, now long for even a single glance from your eyes.
Before him, a kinnarī sings with sweet words, and the beloveds of the gandharvas slowly play musical instruments, standing to his left and right;
celestial women dance before him with the charming sound of tinkling anklets, while Brahmā and the other gods, who are praised by the Vedas, walk around him and offer hymns of praise.

We bow to Sundarī, who bestows upon one who has long served her the attainment of the multitude of great mantras, and who, in due course, grants to another who is free from desire for worldly existence the state whose nature is supreme bliss; and who, resorting to the gateway, gives to yet another—a wretched person whose mind is attached to sense objects—the substance that removes suffering.

I contemplate that primordial Light of supreme splendor, who, having bowed down with a face radiant with love manifested by folded palms, moves slowly and modestly yet with longing into the presence of the Three Oceans;
and who, possessing intense brilliance, explains the entire multitude of various mantras, their meaning, their practice, and their fruit.

O beloved of the Supreme Lord, I bow with intense devotion to the pair of Śarabhas who dwell perpetually at your gate; their terrifying faces, with eyes resembling fire, strike fear into the eyes of all ordinary beings. 72.

At the end of the eon, we bow to the altar in the form of the Śrīcakra, which possesses a splendor equal to many suns risen at once from a single lake; it is adorned with a supreme canopy shimmering with golden cords fastened to jeweled pillars, and features rows of lamps formed by wicks filled with camphor and agallochum, and is radiant with clusters of gems.

O Mother, I perpetually salute the Lion Throne, which is surrounded by hosts of deities stationed in their respective places within the Bindu; which is joyfully established there, shrouded in a downpour of radiant splendor from gold resplendent with various jewels; which is furnished with a seat of a shimmering flower-couch; which is presided over by Kāmeśvara; and which is the source of eternal bliss. (74)

O Daughter of Dakṣa, while the gods joyfully cry "Victory! Victory! on all sides and offer a continuous succession of joined palms with their eyes full of fulfillment, please ascend the golden lion-throne inlaid with circles of many jewels, surrounded by your circle of female companions.

O Beautiful One, we ever salute your handmaidens who stand around your throne, bearing all manner of items such as camphor and other substances, a golden water-pitcher, a jeweled casket for betel-leaf, the hem of a garment, a mirror, and glittering jeweled sandals. 76.

And as the fly-whisks, white as the rays of the full moon, are repeatedly fanned by the attendants holding them—whisks that clearly seem to perform the graceful sport of waving arms with the spreading nets of waves of light from your stainless form—I too move my [own] fly-whisk. 77.

I place upon the Great Lord’s consort a golden parasol, beautiful as the rising orb of the thousand-rayed sun, with its rim shimmering with clusters of pure pearls and its golden handle adorned with gleaming great jewels. 78.

We pay homage to that incomparable and beautiful golden parasol, which has become crimson with the radiance of the mass of red lead from the rising splendor of your body, whose skin resembles a fragment of a lofty ruby, and which is gazed upon from afar by hosts of gods with palms joined in respectful salutation.
With joy, we salute you, the Blessed Lady, who are satisfied with the supreme nectar, who rest in the lap of the radiant Kāmeśvara, and who are worshipped with showers of flowers;

and we reverently bow to the deities stationed within the enclosures of the Śrīcakra, whose individual identities have been attained through their union with the rays emanating from your own body. 80.
O Daughter of the Mountain, having perceived Ādhāraśakti and the others, as well as the supreme Yoginī in the center, and the four Nāthas here beginning with Mitreśanātha— to them I bow.
O Supreme Goddess, I bow to the sixfold seat established within the eight enclosures, beginning from the seat of Tripurasudhārṇava up to Tripuramālinī. 82.

In the northeast, I meditate upon Gaṇeśa, who dispels the darkness of wandering obstacles; in the northwest, I worship Vaṭuka, who has the luster of collyrium and is adorned with a serpent as a sacred thread;
in the southwest, I honor Durgā, the subduer of the demon Mahiṣāsura; and in the southeast, I revere the Lord of the Field (Kṣetrapati), who is intent on protecting all his devotees.

I bow to these seats (pīṭhas) of Uḍḍiyāna, Jālandhara, Kāmarūpa, and Pūrṇagiri, which are situated respectively in the right, front, left, and middle portions of the triangle, and which bestow spiritual accomplishments. 84.

We reverently salute these hosts of gods situated outside the circle—Lokeśa, declared the lord of the earth; Viṣṇu, the master of the waters; Umāpati, the lord of fire; Īśvara, likewise the lord of the winds; and Sadāśiva, the sovereign of space—all of whom have assumed the names of the *pretas*. (85)

I bow to the radiant Sixteen Nityās, preceded by Kāmeśvarī, who have attained great renown throughout the three worlds under the guise of Tārānātha’s introduction to the arts; who have established the sequence of time—down to the divisions of *kalā* and *kāṣṭhā*—within the lunar days (*tithi*); and who are beautiful with jewel ornaments and variegated garments, abiding within the essence of the Cakra. 86.

I bow my head in reverence to the three currents (oghatrika) situated within the sovereign wheel of the lineage of one’s own gurus—a multitude of devotees sustained by diligent instruction and having the deity meditated upon within their hearts. 87.

O Goddess, may this sixfold limb—namely the heart, the head, the crest, the armor for the entire body, and the three eyes, as well as the weapon contemplated by the sages—always manifest within my heart. 88.

I perpetually bow to those mudrās known as the Prakaṭas, who abide upon the three lines of the wheel renowned as Trailokyamohana— the abode of Tripura adorned with shimmering ornaments— and who possess the supernatural powers (siddhis) beginning with Aṇimā.
May the Yoginīs—Kāmākarṣaṇikā and the others—who reside eternally in the Cakra that fulfills all hopes, which shines with a pair of eight petals, and which is the radiant abode of Tripureśvarī;
who are resplendent in divine garments adorned with clusters of jewels; and whose names are both renowned and secret, grant the desired fruit. (90)

In the abode of Tripurasundarī, the Great Goddess who agitates all things, which shines with eight petals and is radiant with a multitude of ornaments, may Anaṅgakusumā and the others—resplendent with various decorations, both subtle and those bearing secret names—grant my desire. (91)

May all the Siddhis—whose names are known through the established traditions and whose faces begin with "Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī," the "Auspicious One who Agitates All"—bestow auspiciousness. They reside in the temple of the Dweller of Tripura, which is adorned with beautiful ornaments and shines with the eight spokes of the wheel of action, bestowing every form of good fortune.
May those who abide in Tripurā, known as Kulakaulas, who grant all perfections, protect [us] within the outer ten-spoked wheel that accomplishes all aims. || 93 ||

I perpetually salute the one known as Nigarbha, who dwells eternally within the exceedingly charming eight-petalled lotus that adorns the interior, which provides protection to all from the beginning, whose abode was fashioned by Mālinī, Tripurā, and others; he is adorned with various jewels, resplendent with clusters of gems, clothed in divine raiment, and is constantly surrounded by the multitude of powers (Śaktis) such as Sarvajñā.
I perpetually bow to Vaśinī and the other secret Yoginīs, who reside within the eight-spoked [cakra] that removes all diseases and is endowed with the accomplishment of Tripurā.

O Supreme Śivā, I bow to Your weapons stationed within the intervals of the [five] discs: the beautiful flower-bow, the exquisite noose, and likewise the goad, fashioned from arrows consisting of blossoms shining with the pollen of mango, aśoka, and vikāsika flowers, as well as blue lotuses and blooming fresh jasmine.
May Kāmeśvarī, who dwells with Ambā Tripurā in this world that has arisen like a triangle and bestows all accomplishments, grant me auspiciousness;
may Vajreśvarī grant me every well-being, and may Bhagamālinī manifest within my mind. 97.

May that Yoginī protect me—she who dwells in the abode fashioned by Bhairavī Tripurā and others within the Bindu, which consists of all bliss and is desired by the entire world; she whose eyes shine with joy, who is adorned with garments and ornaments resplendent with clusters of jewels, and whose face is radiant; she who is both supreme and non-supreme, the secret essence. 98.
O Goddess, I offer to you this campaka flower, which is radiant with the splendor of shimmering gold and perfumes the air with its throbbing fragrance, yet has been avoided from afar by the bees. 99.

Having cast aside his fierce anger, Śambhu placed upon his head a *ketakī* flower under the guise of a crescent moon; I ever offer that very flower to you, which is frequented by bees greedy for its fragrance.

I offer to you this mass of blossoming jasmine flowers held clearly in my joined palms; it is as if the orb of the moon, which vies with your face, has been instantly pulverized by the Lotus-born Brahmā.

I place upon the pedestal of my neck a garland of *vakula* flowers—a garland whose radiance rivals a row of emerald gems, delightful with the constant fragrance of thick agaru incense, and which attracts swarms of bees drawn by its scent spreading in every direction and intermediate quarter. (102)

The syllable *īṃ* consists of the upper bindu as the face and the two lower bindus as the breasts; this entire form, consisting of lines within the heart, is accessible to the Guru throughout the three worlds.
Thus, worshipping the Blessed Lady who is the essence of the Kāmakalā within, may the virtuous person attain the thrill of bliss while immersed in the ocean of bliss. 103.
O Blessed One, I offer you incense born of agaru wood, overflowing with its exalted fragrance, and likewise a lamp that dispels the darkness of the heart with its brilliance.
O beautiful one, whose nature is supreme bliss, I present to you the food offering placed in vessels made of gold and silver set all around. 104.
This pure, clean rice, resembling jasmine buds, is placed in a golden vessel; likewise, there are soups made from mung beans, black gram, and chickpeas.
This excellent ghee—cow's butter, buffalo butter, and even goat's butter—is presented in separate vessels. O Supreme Śiva, please accept all of this.

O Girijā, I reverently present before you in a multitude of golden vessels these divine dishes—śimbī, sūraṇa, śāka, bimba, bṛhatī, kūśmāṇḍa, kośātakī, vṛntāka, and paṭola—all prepared with a gentle fire and seasoned with an abundance of vesavāra. (106)

O Girijā, I offer to you, whose blissful form is consciousness, various kinds of medicinal preparations (*saṃdhāna*) prepared with lime, ginger, mango, tuberous roots, plantain, *kauśātakī*, cucumber, *dhātrī*, *bilva*, and *karīra*, seasoned with rows of mustard seeds, pungent oil, rock salt, and turmeric; may these be accepted by you. 107.
O Pārvatī, out of affection I offer to you these clusters of sweetmeat balls requested from Sitā, soft cakes, tender *pūrikās*, and this supreme rice dish.
O Mother, I offer to you all this: ghee well-prepared in fire, curds resembling the orb of the moon, molasses, and *śikhariṇī* sweetened with both sugar and honey. 109.

O Mother, O Queen of Gods, beloved of Śambhu, having first offered all this immeasurable *naivedya* before You and knowing that the fourfold reality has been accepted, I consider You, the Goddess, to be fully satiated; thereafter, I present the remainder placed in golden vessels as offerings to the *Śaktis*. 110.

I bow to Annapūrṇā, who stands before you, intoxicated with the joy of wine; she holds in her left hand a golden vessel filled with incomparable, supreme food, and in her other hand a golden ladle that grants the heart’s desires to her own people; her body is dark-hued, her garments are red as vermilion, and she is adorned with beautiful ornaments of various gems. || 111 ||
O Mother, having worshipped with devotion and all ritual offerings those attendants of yours who are seated in rows around the circle, their left sides embraced by your own Śakti, I bow down to them.

We worship that supreme light, resplendent as the sun, situated in the midst of a host of beautiful women intoxicated by the supreme nectar, its eyes rolling from the intoxication of that supreme nectar. 113.
O Śivā, your lotus-face is seen, and the clear sound of the unstruck drum (anāhata) is heard;
while worshipping you, who are beyond the reach of words, the mind does not wander toward other objects. 114.
O Supreme Goddess, I perceive this assembly of yours as having attained the state of *unmanī*, for their pair of eyes are fixed and motionless in love upon beholding the lotus of your face. 115.
Let the eye see nothing else here, nor let the nose smell, nor indeed let the ear hear; alas, let even the skin not cling to touch.
Let the tongue not taste flavor; rather, O Supreme One, whose eyes are reeling with eternal bliss, let my mind eternally immerse itself in Your essential nature.

O Pārvatī, O beautiful one, I believe that he who beholds you daily through meditation as composed of radiant light has reached the ultimate conclusion regarding this entire reality found within the Vedas.
At that moment, when my heart was saturated with bliss during the rite of your worship, I attained non-difference from you, O Supreme Śivā; this indeed is your grace.

Having worshipped with all ritual offerings and with devotion, we present the bali-oblation according to the prescribed methods to Gaṇādhinātha, Vaṭuka, the Yoginīs, and Kṣetrādhinātha in the four intermediate directions.
Having indeed offered the remains to Śeṣikā, who is playing the lute nearby,
perform the pure ritual rinsing of the mouth with water poured from a golden pitcher.
I offer betel-leaf, beautifully prepared with camphor, musk, nutmeg, areca nut, cloves, and catechu powder, presented with devotion;
please accept this *ārārtika* ceremony, radiant with lamps placed within shimmering jewel caskets and fashioned from powdered rice. 120.
O Mother, one Kinnarī sings with melodious words while Urvaśī and Rambhā play musical instruments and dance with playful, charming steps before you.
Casting aside their duties, the celestial women gaze upon and behold your face—the ocean of the nectar of eternal bliss—with eyes rolling from the intoxication of wine.

It was being heard by the hosts of Śaktis stationed in the circle, whose faces were radiant with betel-leaf, whose eyes were gladdened by the sight of your stainless countenance, and who had abandoned attachment to sense objects.
In the ritual of worship, even a fragment of knowledge is far, far away, as are all things that might bring it about;
therefore, having circumambulated You, I offer this worship consisting of the five-fold service (pañcopacāra).

Worshipped with services manifested according to my heart's desire, surrounded by the host of deities of your own retinue, and seated upon the throne of the Lord of the Gods—I, repeatedly joining my palms in reverence and touching the ground with the eight limbs of my body, bow down to you, O Blessed Tripurasundarī; protect me! 124.
Pay heed to my petition with great effort; O Mother, do not now cast aside me who have come into your presence and am now distraught.

If my mind should ever stray from the contemplation of your feet, or if my sight and speech should ever wander, then, O Compassionate One, bind them with your own virtues so that they may never depart again.

Where am I, of dull intellect, and where is this worship of the Śrīpādukā with my own mind, which has been praised and meditated upon by all those exclusively devoted to You? Nevertheless, O Goddess, I believe that this hymn, which bestows happiness, was revealed by that Deity through my mouth, as She was pleased by my occasional practice of contemplation.
May Sundarī favor this daily worship, which has been composed by me in various verses and is constantly meditated upon within my mind. 127.

Thus ends the *Tripurasundarīmānasapūjāstotra*, composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the illustrious wandering mendicant teacher (paramahaṃsaparivrājakācārya) and disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda.
